Corfu Old Sephardic Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kerkira, Greece

Demolished. Corfu's Jewish community, blending Romaniot, Italian, and Sephardi traditions after successive waves of immigration, developed a unique liturgical tradition known as the Corfu Rite (Minhag Corfu) that preserved Greek Jewish customs for centuries. Among its most notable residents was Yitzhak Abravanel, the renowned statesman and biblical scholar, who wrote his commentary on the Book of Isaiah here before moving on to Venice. The community peaked at 6,000 people in 1863 and remained one of Greece's larger Jewish populations into the 20th century, until German bombing in 1943 destroyed the Italian community's three synagogues and, in May 1944, roughly 1,800 Jews were deported to Auschwitz by freight train; only a small community, rebuilt partly by survivors from elsewhere, remained afterward. This cemetery, presumed established in the late 15th century for the community's Sephardi congregation, has been completely demolished; a school, a fire station, a parking lot, and residential buildings now stand on the site.
